beats.trigger: From Personal to Team
beats.got: nothing new, just a title

beats.trigger: You can't really share an agent.
beats.got: you can only share context, a skill, output or an interface, and picking one is the actual decision

beats.trigger: Bring one example from your own organisation of access without use: a tool people can open and mostly don't.
beats.got: homework. i have copilot seats nobody opens, so i know the answer already

beats.trigger: **Interview** for the job a teammate is trying to get done before deciding what to share
beats.got: nothing new, a list of verbs. interviewing before building is the part i usually skip

beats.trigger: What would you want a teammate to actually have: your folder, one of your skills, the morning output, or a way to ask it a question in Slack?
beats.got: i have to pick between four shapes of sharing, and i'd have said 'the folder' without thinking

beats.trigger: Hold the impulse.
beats.got: it tells me to start from the teammate's job, which i'd normally skip. fair, but i want to build

beats.trigger: This is a heavy read across the working set, and a shallow confident finish is as risky as over-reading.
beats.got: the agent can quit reading too early and sound sure about it, so you have to push it. i've seen that, but a pasted prompt is a pasted prompt

beats.trigger: Schedule the agent. Output lands where the team looks.
beats.got: push means the sales team never runs an agent, they just get the output. that's the only version i can see non-engineers using

beats.trigger: You now have the teammate's job and a candidate selected against it.
beats.got: nothing new, just a bridge to the next exercise

beats.trigger: Now find the obstacle that decides whether the teammate can actually absorb it, then draft both halves of the plan.
beats.got: find the real blocker and write two plans, one technical and one for people

beats.trigger: A good bottleneck explains why several other obstacles stay hard.
beats.got: look for the one blocker that keeps the others hard, not the first technical limit. reasonable, but i skimmed the review step

beats.trigger: A polished technical file beside a people file full of unnamed roles is the finding, not a finished rollout.
beats.got: my rollouts look exactly like that: a great technical file and nobody named as owner or maintainer

beats.trigger: checks the assumptions underneath these plans, imagines the failure, and writes the first real-world contact
beats.got: nothing new, another bridge

beats.trigger: The technical and people plans are hypotheses.
beats.got: the plans are guesses, so test them

beats.trigger: what would have to be true for this teammate, doing this job, to fire their current hire and use my candidate?
beats.got: your agent is competing with whatever they use today, so ask what would make them drop that. i hadn't framed it that way

beats.trigger: Six months from now, the teammate went back to the incumbent.
beats.got: a premortem where the sales team quietly goes back to their spreadsheet, which is a likely outcome of my weekend build

beats.trigger: A candidate picked because it fits the infrastructure is shopping.
beats.got: i pick by what fits the stack, and that's shopping, not design. fine, it stings a bit

beats.trigger: Sharing an agent runs into one law.
beats.got: nothing yet, but 'one law' sounds like a big claim

beats.trigger: The fourth does not copy at all, which is why the product being sold as a shared agent is always three of the four parts, with the fourth still sitting with whoever built it.
beats.got: context, boundary and checks copy easily. accountability doesn't, and it stays with whoever built the thing, which would be me

beats.trigger: The person who wants your folder is rarely the person who wants a Slack bot.
beats.got: nothing new, the four strategies again with who each suits. i know my engineers want the folder

beats.trigger: Many companies have rolled out access far ahead of trust.
beats.got: turning on a licence takes a minute, while people actually using it takes weeks and gets reported as one number

beats.trigger: Name what was switched on, and when.
beats.got: nothing new, it's the prework again

beats.trigger: The leadership had not done the analysis. People they trusted had.
beats.got: a multi-agent value-stream redesign with 15 people was good, and leadership still didn't decide because they hadn't done the analysis themselves. that's the org-wide failure mode i haven't hit yet

beats.trigger: Somebody they trust has to have used it first and said so.
beats.got: the switch conditions are small things: lands where they look, right the first time, and someone they trust vouching for it

beats.trigger: Ask the question before you show them anything you built.
beats.got: talk to one person about how they work before demoing. i'd normally demo first

beats.trigger: Compare your choice with a neighbour's, then run the debrief.
beats.got: nothing new, chat with the neighbour then another prompt

beats.trigger: Test the switch, not the solution.
beats.got: a recap. that line is the only one i'd repeat

beats.trigger: One real conversation tells you more about absorption than a finished plan does.
beats.got: I'm supposed to talk to a real person before next time. i'll see

beats.trigger: In Module 8 you ask what changes when you don't have to build each one by hand.
beats.got: module 8 is about not hand-building each agent, which is the part i actually want

take_homes: you can't hand someone your agent. you share context, a skill, output or an interface, and push or pull means they never have to run an agent
turning access on is easy, but people using it is slow and belongs to them. i'd better name who owns and maintains the thing before i build it
ask what the person does today before showing them anything, and what would make them drop it

monday.move: message one person in sales and ask for 20 minutes on how they prep for a customer call today. no demo and no building
monday.who: head of sales, or whoever she says actually does the prep
monday.when: monday morning, before i open claude code, and probably a quick meeting later in the week
monday.stop_condition: if their current way is fine or nobody there cares, i drop the org-wide sales setup
monday.blocker: nobody outside engineering asked for it, and i haven't found out who would maintain it. i'll also be tempted to build a prototype first anyway

misconception.why: the module barely touches whether agent output is correct. it was about who adopts it. i skipped the 'read the file' review steps and nothing changed my mind. the 'unnamed roles' line hit my rollout habits, but not 'checking is for beginners'

one_line: good for the rollout part, the scar story and the 'what would make them switch' question are worth it, but half of it re-explains what i already do daily and i skipped most of the review steps
